hosts.name: Linda Carducci
hosts.bio: Linda Carducci is the weekday morning host on WETA Classical. She received classical training on piano and hosted a daily classical music program in Pittsburgh prior to coming to WETA.

hosts.name: Bill Bukowski
hosts.bio: Bill Bukowski is the weekday midday host on WETA Classical. He came to WETA in 2013 from WSCL on the Delmarva pennisula. In his spare time he enjoys playing guitar, mountain dulcimer and ukulele.

hosts.name: Nicole Lacroix
hosts.bio: Nicole Lacroix is the weekday afternoon host on WETA Classical. Lacroix spent fifteen years at the former WGMS in Washington, with stints at VOA, KDFC San Francisco and at Baltimore's WJHU and WBJC.

hosts.name: James Jacobs

hosts.name: John Banther

hosts.name: Rich Kleinfeldt

hosts.name: Evan Keely

hosts.name: Austin Vitaliano

hosts.name: Chip Brienza

hosts.name: Matthew Dayton

hosts.name: David Martosko
hosts.bio: David Martosko is a journalist and writer who was trained on the piano, cello, and tuba but sang his way through his teens and ultimately embraced opera — first on stage and then on the podium.

hosts.name: Marcus Pfeifer

articles.title: Matthew White on WNO's Madama Butterfly
articles.dek: James Jacobs speaks with tenor Matthew White about the Washington National Opera's production of Puccini's Madama Butterfly.
articles.body:
Matthew White, who’s currently singing the role of B. F. Pinkerton in Washington National Opera’s production of Puccini’s Madama Butterfly, didn’t start studying voice until he was nineteen. Before that he played several different instruments in a variety of styles and genres, though classical violin was what he assumed would be his main focus as his teens progressed and he thought about college and career. But when he decided to switch his attention to his voice, he dropped out of college and performed manual labor to support his voice lessons, focusing exclusively on technique for three years before considering repertoire. This bold move paid off; he went on to win a slew of competitions and enjoy a still-ascendant career. (You can find out more in my illuminating interview with him embedded above.) His performance as Pinkerton marks his WNO debut.

Image

And what a debut it is! I had the privilege of attending the dress rehearsal. The WNO has transformed the cavernous DAR Constitution Hall into their “Revolutionary Stage”, designed by Walt Spangler, whose work has been seen at many DC venues. The orchestra is placed on the back of the stage in full view of the audience, while the action takes place on a thrust stage jutting out into the hall, surrounded on three sides by audience members sitting at tables where they can enjoy refreshments purchased at the bar, and get a very close look at some cast members who occasionally enter and exit through the audience. While I’ve seen the “immersive theatre” approach work well for comedies and experimental pieces, it was astonishing to see how well it worked for one of opera’s starkest and most period-specific tragedies. Madama Butterfly cannot be about anything except the clash of Japanese and American cultures in Nagasaki at the dawn of the 20th century (during a panel discussion with the production’s creative team, the director E. Loren Meeker joked that “we’re not setting this on the moon in ape suits”), and they managed to conjure that period with evocative costumes by the legendary Broadway designer Florence Klotz. There was also beautiful dancing, choreographed by Kanji Segawa, that eloquently embodied Cio-Cio San’s emotional state in kinesthetic terms. The orchestra, put front and center as it should be, sounded magnificent under the baton of Erina Yashima.

Image Pinkerton (Matthew White), Cio-Cio San (Karah Son)/Photo credit: Cory Weaver

In vocal terms Cio-Cio San was portrayed by Korean soprano Karah Son, who, like Matthew White, is making a powerful WNO debut in this production. Equally striking were the performances of longtime WNO stalwart Michelle Mariposa as Suzuki and the Grammy-winning Will Liverman as Sharpless.

If you’ve never seen or listened to Madama Butterfly, it’s not much of a spoiler to say that it lacks a happy ending. But its ravishing catharsis epitomizes what opera is about – especially in a production such as this that combines solid musicianship and production values with a thrilling handmade quality as it seems to come to life right in front of you.

The interview can also be heard on WETA Virtuoso on the following times:

articles.title: DC Composer James Lee III
articles.dek: Linda Carducci speaks with Maryland-based composer James Lee III about his visions and influences, his compositions, and his thoughts for the evolving nature of Classical music.
articles.body:
If you attend concerts in the Washington area, chances are you’ve heard the sensitive and inventive music of composer James Lee III. The Maryland-based composer’s works, ranging from orchestral and chamber music to pieces for piano, voice and chorus, have been showcased internationally and described by The Washington Post as "bright, pure music" Major American orchestras, including the National Symphony Orchestra and the Detroit Symphony Orchestra have championed Mr. Lee’s works, and he served as composer-in-residence with the Baltimore Symphony Orchestra for the 2024-2025 season.

As part of our local composers’ spotlight this month of November, we’re pleased to showcase compositions of James Lee III on WETA Classical and WETA’s HD channel, Virtuoso. He discusses his visions and influences, his compositions, and his thoughts for the evolving nature of Classical music, in my conversation with him below.

articles.title: Opera Lafayette Celebrates Rameau 350
articles.dek: James Jacobs speaks with Artistic Director of Opera Lafayette, Patrick Dupre Quigley, about their Rameau 350 project, starting with Les Surprises des l'Amour this month.
articles.body:
Last month the hot ticket in DC was Oliver Cotton’s play The Score, which took place in 1747. Ostensibly the origin story for Johann Sebastian Bach’s Musical Offering, its climactic scene depicted Bach confronting Frederick the Great about the brutal effects his military campaign had on ordinary citizens.

In the following year, 1748, the War of Austrian Succession finally ended with Aix-la-Chapelle, which also has connections to notable musical compositions. In England, Handel composed the Music for the Royal Fireworks to commemorate the event (and while its premiere resulted in war-like consequences that seemed at odds with its celebration of piece – a building burned down, at least five people suffered serious injuries, and it caused one of the first recorded traffic jams – everyone still liked the music.)

In France, meanwhile, King Louis XV’s illustrious mistress Madame de Pompadour was running her third season of opera and drama in a makeshift theater in her apartment at Versailles. The venue’s very limited seating made admission extremely coveted among the Parisian aristocracy, and while their desire to attend may have been driven by social status, they were from all reports performances of very high quality, including onstage appearances by the Madame herself.

The Aix-la-Chapelle treaty inspired her to commission the most successful living French composer at the time, Jean-Philippe Rameau, for an opera. While his works for the Paris Opéra could run three hours or more, for this occasion he provided a 90-minute work in a prologue and two acts, Les surprises de l'Amour. The one character who ties the work together is Cupid; in the prologue it is revealed that Vulcan’s arrows of war are transformed into Cupid’s arrows of love. The theme of the opera is that love is the rebuke to the cold-heartedness that leads to war – a powerful statement for a mistress to present to the King.

After its initial performance in Madame de Pompadour’s apartment, Les surprises de l'Amour was heavily revised and expanded for performance at the Paris Opéra, and all of its references to the peace treaty were cut. While this later version has been revived and recorded in modern times, the more intimate and philosophical original version has lain on the shelf – until now. Opera Lafayette is giving what it is billing as the “modern world premiere” of the original version of 1748.

I got to speak with Patrick Dupre Quigley, Opera Lafayette’s new artistic director, about this production and their Rameau350 project in a fascinating interview you can hear above.

The interview can be heard on WETA Virtuoso on the following times:

articles.title: Bayreuth at 150: Curious Choices
articles.dek: Ahead of the broadcast of Wagner's Rienzi on WETA Classical's Opera Matinee on November 14, Jim Allison shares his reflections on this year's Bayreuth Festival after attending the 150th-anniversary season.
articles.body:
This weekend on WETA Classical’s Opera Matinee, we have the rare opportunity to hear a production of Richard Wagner’s Rienzi from the Bayreuth Festival in Germany. I say “rare” because this early Wagner opera had never been presented inside the Bayreuth Festspielhaus (Festival Theatre) until this summer, when it opened the festival’s 150th-anniversary season. I also say “rare” with a glimmer of hope that this will be the only time Rienzi appears in the festival’s official lineup.

That said, you’re in for a fine performance on Saturday. Nathalie Stutzmann conducts, with acclaimed Wagnerian tenor Andreas Schager in the title role.

However, the fact remains that Wagner wished Rienzi and his other apprentice operas not to be presented at the Festspielhaus. It was a wish that his descendants respected until now. From my standpoint as an audience member and frequent attendee, I think it should have continued to be honored.

Rienzi remained popular in Europe well after Wagner’s death. Still, it is French-style grand opera, a long way from Wagner’s mature style and his revolutionary concept of music and drama. It was for his later works that Wagner designed the Festspielhaus, with its iconic sunken, covered orchestra pit. That feature, so important in creating a unique balance between a massive Wagnerian orchestra and the singers, placed the much smaller Rienzi orchestra at a disadvantage. At least, that was my experience in the audience back in August. On Saturday’s broadcast, we can all listen for how grand-opera orchestration fares in a pit designed for something else.

Image Rienzi, Gabriela Scherer (Irene), Jennifer Holloway (Adriano)/Photo Credit: Bayreuther Festspiele / Enrico Nawrath

Beyond these quibbles, I came away feeling that the care and resources went to the wrong anniversary. Rienzi, a work Wagner kept out of the house, received an elaborate, fully staged production. The Ring, the work the Festspielhaus was built for, received a concept in which the singers mostly stood and sang while AI and video screens did the rest.

One often leaves a Bayreuth production puzzling over staging choices. Yes, a new production of the Ring was presented this summer, but the AI-generated staging was beyond disappointing; it was distracting and undramatic. The concept was to feed images from earlier Bayreuth productions and 150 years of Ring reception history into an AI system and let it generate the visuals during each performance. The creators have said it was an experiment, not a stage-directed drama, and it looked like one.

Image Das Rheingold/Photo Credit: Bayreuther Festspiele / Enrico Nawrath

Aside from projections of the original 1876 staging at the beginning of each act, the images rarely connected to the words or music, and the singers were given scant opportunities to act. In fact, during long stretches of the performances the singers, standing in a “park-and-bark” stance in uniform, shimmering costumes, disappeared into the video projections. For many of us, it is to experience the artistry of the musicians that we travel to Bayreuth and sit in the un-air-conditioned Festspielhaus (this year during an unrelenting heat wave). Minimizing the visual presence of the singers on the stage felt like disrespect for their all-important roles.

Image Siegfried/Photo Credit: Bayreuther Festspiele / Enrico Nawrath

Since AI was at the center of this project, I asked Claude, an AI assistant made by Anthropic, for its view. It cautioned that it hadn’t seen the staging, but put the problem less in the technology than in the framing: an experiment presented as the anniversary Ring, to an audience expecting a staging. My own takeaway: the question isn’t whether AI can stage an opera. It’s whether such an experiment should be the anniversary Ring.

Visual disappointments aside, this summer’s Ring was musically excellent, with Christian Thielemann’s conducting and Michael Volle’s Wotan/Wanderer at its center. I have found the musical artistry at Bayreuth a wonderfully consistent reason to return, even if some of the stagings are less than satisfying.

Unfortunately, the Ring wasn’t available to us for broadcast, but I hope you enjoy the rare presentation of Rienzi on November 14th at 1:00 p.m. on WETA Classical. It’s a great opportunity to hear an excellent cast and some hints of the mature Wagner to come.

articles.title: Forward Thinking Opera Company IN Series' New Home in Southwest DC
articles.dek: Evan Keely speaks with IN Series Artistic Director Timothy Nelson about the exciting new chapter of a permanent home at Revada Performing Arts Center in SW DC.
articles.body:
In the history of arts in our nation’s capital, I expect that October 23, 2026 will be a date remembered with appreciation: the date of the Ribbon Cutting for the Revada Arts Center.

This new arts hub in the SW neighborhood, around the corner from the Waterfront Metro stop, will be the home of Theater Alliance, the 4EYE Film Center, and the opera company IN Series. It is the product of the visionary aspirations of the creatives in these three organizations and the surrounding community, and of the generous responses to a $4.5 million capital campaign.

I spoke with Timothy Nelson, Artistic Director of IN Series, about this exciting new development.

Image Timothy Nelson addresses crowd at Revada Arts Center Opening Ceremony

Evan Keely: Let me start by offering my heartiest congratulations to you, IN Series, Theater Alliance, 4EYE Film Center and the good folks in this SW Washington neighborhood on this thrilling new development: the opening of the Revada Arts Center. I appreciated the conversation you and I had in March about it; I was not aware at that point in time (and perhaps no one was then?) of what the name of this new arts hub would be. At WETA Classical, this name is familiar to us, in no small part because the Revada Foundation is an underwriter of Opera at Eight on WETA VivaLaVoce. What do you want the community to know about the name “Revada Arts Center”?

Timothy Nelson: First of all, I think it’s important for folks to know what this means for IN Series. We’ve not only been nomadic or itinerant for most of our life as an arts institution, but we’ve been proudly so. It’s deeply meaningful to be able to think about what pieces will speak most impactfully in what communities and in what types of spaces. For instance, recently producing Bernstein’s MASS in a sacred space totally changed the way that colossal work spoke to its audience, as a spiritual experience in a way, at least for me, it has always fallen flat in the concert hall. Being at home at the REVADA ARTS CENTER means producing largely in the same DC theater space. Importantly, we will continue to do one site-specific production each season (this year’s THE TRIUMPH OF F.A.U.V.E.L. - An Ass! is notably at the Dupont Underground) because we think that sort of work matters. Being in a space that is a known-quantity for the rest of our season, at least for now, allows us to not have to re-invent the wheel for each project, and to instead focus on a journey of growth in terms of artistic excellent, production acumen, and administrative strength as we seek to evolve from a DC arts organization, to a real institution, a pillar of the DC arts eco-system, and as THE second company in DC’s opera landscape.

EK: IN Series is not a stranger to this space: I appreciated hearing and seeing The Delta King’s Blues there last season; the ongoing renovation of the facility was clearly visible then. You and I spoke last June about Sic Semper Tyrannis, the 2026–27 season for IN Series, but please tell us about the first IN Series production that will be mounted at the new Revada Arts Center.

TN: Our first production in the new space, also our first production of 2027 which is our 45th anniversary year, captures the heart of IN Series — it is made of works never heard before by most DC audiences, it is wholly original and unexpected, it is strange and spiritual and absurd and full

of wonder and surprise. It is also one of the largest projects musically and visually we’ve ever mounted. Un-subtlely titled (N)O KING(S), its first half merges three of the great modernist vocal works of the 20th century into a sort of “requiem for the American dream”, the 20th century itself as the “great American century”. King Harald’s Saga is an acapella one-woman opera depicting King Harald of Norway’s futile attempt to lay siege to England at the Battle of Hasting, but is really an examination of the futility of war and indictment of the Vietnam conflict during which it was written. 8 Songs for a Mad King is the most famous work on the program, and is Peter Maxwell Davies’s incredible setting of texts inspired by the diary entries of the mad King George III on losing the American colonies. Finally, Luciano Berio’s O King was written for the death of Martin Luther King and is simply the intoning of the vowels of the slain leader’s name. Together these works will become a meditation on what has brought America to this point. The second half is the American fully staged premiere of George Benjamin’s Into the Little Hill, the first operatic masterpiece of the 21st century, which sets the story of the Pied Piper as an indictment of societies that send away migrant populations and refuse to pay for the arts — they lose their children, their souls. This is how IN Series marks the anniversary of our country, in ways which we hope move beyond ceremony and pomp and towards meaningful reflection and contemplation.

EK: Something caught my eye on the Revada Arts Center website: IN Series, Theater Alliance and 4EYE Film Center are cited not as “partners”, but “core partners”. That “core” seems to me to have implications that I find quite exciting: it suggests that these organizations are central, but that the partnerships will extend beyond just three institutions. Can you tell us more about that? And now that this new arts hub is a reality (complete with ribbon cutting and a launch weekend, October 23–27), has your own vision grown and deepened for what kinds of partnerships and possibilities lie ahead for IN Series?

TN: The new center has three core partners, and we look forward to sharing resources and knowledge, but also programming in conversation with each other to actively create deeper and deeper context to our work. Additionally, with three very distinct audiences, we look forward to opportunities for these audiences to mix and meld together. There will be other partners that use the space with a lower level of commitment, but with an equally shared set of values and priorities. We aren’t quite ready yet to announce those partnerships, but we will be soon. And then the space is available for community use, additional artistic experiences, co-working, and shared hospitality.

EK: A development — related or not to this new arts hub coming into existence now, I’m not so sure, but I suspect so — that I also find really exciting is how IN Series continues to expand its geographic scope: in addition to performances in the DMV, not only at the Revada Arts Center but, for instance, your recent debut at Arena Stage, you’re continuing to partner with the Baltimore Theater Project for performances there (that’s where I saw your opera The Song of Sakuntala); the stagings of The Triumph of F.A.U.V.E.L. — An Ass! — which is, among other things, a collaboration with the Brooklyn-based medieval music ensemble Alkemie — will include a performance in New York. Do you envision having an established home base at the Revada Arts Center as an opportunity for continuing this kind of growth?

TN: We believe in the total uniqueness of IN Series work, certainly in DC and the area, but also nationally and even internationally. My dream for as long as I can remember is to have a company with a stable of regular artists that tours a body of work throughout the world. Partnering is also central to our identity, so being able to create work with Alkemie and then perform in New York is a step along that journey, and just the beginning as this is intentional and part of our long term strategic vision.

EK: As the conversation between you and me has unfolded over the past year, both of us have faced this development with great anticipation, but now that it’s real, have any of your views changed? Do you foresee possibilities for the 2027–28 season (and beyond) for IN Series that you haven’t before? And/or: do you find renewed courage and/or ongoing challenges as you think about what’s going to be possible for IN Series?

TN: I think being forced to wear an administrative hat was well as an artistic hat keeps me honest and balanced. I’m always seeing opportunities in challenges, and risks in possible rewards, both ways. It’s a sort of vigilant optimism that is fundamental to my world view as an artist and a person. New ideas have emerged and old ideas have evolved or even placed on hold for the moment, only to emerge when their time has come. Overall, however, the sense of true possibility this moment holds hasn’t dampened at all and we’re all incredibly eager to wander somewhat with a sense of where we are going, and somewhat enjoying being a little lost, towards the future.

articles.title: DC Composer Greg Sandow
articles.dek: James Jacobs speaks with DC-based composer Greg Sandow about his works and highlights his album "Three Quartets" recorded by Terra String Quartet.
articles.body:
Greg Sandow has degrees from Harvard and Yale and has taught at Juilliard, Eastman and Peabody. He began his musical life as a singer and focused on composition in college, but he spent most of his career as a writer. He was the classical music critic for the Village Voice and a regular contributor to the Wall Street Journal, and he's also written about pop music and scientific phenomena. This vibrant 83-year-old Washington, D.C. resident has turned his focus back to composition, and I recently spoke to him about a new album of his string quartets performed by the Terra String Quartet. While the three works were conceived separately, Mr. Sandow was pleased to discover how well they work as an album.

Image

The matching of performers to composer was serendipitous; the quartet’s violinists Harriet Langley and Amelia Dietrich were both students in Mr. Sandow’s courses at Juilliard. And while he insists he’s no longer in the business of pontificating about The State of Classical Music, everything about this recording reflects his values and aesthetics that feels like a statement and not just a product.

The album opens with Quartet for Anne, (2001) which he wrote as a birthday present for his then-new wife Anne Midgette (former music critic for the Washington Post, who, like her husband, is making a career turn from critic to creator and is currently working on a novel), a work full of beauty accessible to all as well as references only she would get. The Remembered Song (2018) is a metaphysical meditation on the music one dimly remembers from a previous existence. Mahler Variations (2004), by far the longest work, consists of 22 variations on the final movement of Mahler’s Third Symphony. Many of the variations are dedicated to specific artists, mostly composers, but also a couple of film directors, and the longest variation of all is titled Proust, based on the famous opening passage of Swann’s Way, which you can hear Mr. Sandow reading in the illuminating interview you can hear above.

articles.title: The Revada Arts Center: A brand-new home for the arts in Southwest DC
articles.dek: Nicole Lacroix speaks with Theater Alliance's executive artistic director Shanara Gabrielle about the opening of a new performing arts space in Southwest DC.
articles.body:
In February of 2025, I happened to be walking home from the library, when I noticed a sign for a play being presented that afternoon by Theater Alliance. The play, "Garbologists," was held in a pop-up black box in the bowels of a brand-new apartment building. This summer, in Waterfront Park, Theater Alliance presented a Woody Guthrie musical. Now, with the grand opening of the Revada Arts Center, Theater Alliance is no longer relagated to pop-ups or the great outdoors.

I met with Theater Alliance's executive artistic director Shanara Gabrielle, a magnetic and passionate advocate, to tour the new complex. We discussed her dreams for this collaborative concept which also includes two other partners, the innovative opera company, INSeries and 4 Eye Film Center (named after the address, 4th and I streets).

We began the tour in the lobby, or as Shanara put it:

"This is the "radical hospitality hub," this will be our co-working and artist networking space as well as our café and community space. We'll have community meetings, really nice coffee and a bar also in the evening. This is also where we hope, when people come to a show, that they want to stay and have a conversation afterwards....that's one of our greatest hopes, that you leave with more questions than you came with."

Nicole Lacroix: During the week, Thursday-Sunday noon to 10 pm, the hub is open to both community and artists...it's a third space where you can bring your computer, get a cup of coffee or tea and absorb the artistic vibes.

There's a grille above the bar on the mezzanine level, where you can watch the labor that goes into producing the plays and operas.

Next, Shanara took me through a portal into the main performance space, the fully-equipped Black Box which seats 140.

Image

Shanara Gabrielle: It's the entrance into your story...every time you come, it's a different set up...[we] want the audience to have a very fresh experience every time they arrive.

NL: The center is 9000 square feet, "every square inch" of which, as Shanara said, is dedicated to making art. She took me through to Theater 2, a film screening room with stadium seating which also doubles as an intimate space for smaller performances. We walked by rehearsal rooms, a green room, a costume shop and spanking new restrooms, a major relief for theatergoers who remember having to use the preschool next door!

Back in the conference room, we talked shop:

SG: We launched our capital campaign in July of last year, so it's15 months of raising money to make it happen. We started to build 5 months ago and it's now open and complete tomorrow.

NL: I'm thinking it took 5 months to renovate our kitchen, which gives you an idea of Shanara's dynamic leadership. She continued:

SG: Theater Alliance has the lease on the building, so we're the owner of the space, and we did the capital campaign and raised all the money to build the space. There's a financial responsibility that Theater Alliance has both to the developer and to the Southwest community (for space-use requirements). So, after that financial structure, the thing we want to do is internally create a collective cooperative structure for how the space works. That's when Theater Alliance brought INSeries and 4EYE Film Center as our core partners. (although there is a second tier of 3 smaller organizations to come later in the year.)

NL: Theater Alliance has been active for 25 years, first in the H Street area then in Anacostia, and now in SW Washington in a flourishing location a block from the Waterfront Metro, near theater, music, Nationals Park, Audi Field, the Smithsonian and a plethora of restaurants.

SG: We're thinking what an arts district looks like: down from the Mall to the Rubell, to here, to Arena Stage, to Pearl St. to the Anthem-- you've got a little walking path of arts here, and we're very excited to connect with other organizations.

NL: Is this a new model for the arts?

SG: I really do think it is a new model. I think the thing that makes us different is a couple of pretty radical financial ideas.

Everybody pays the same rate. It's the square footage divided by the amount of time that you're going to use it over time. There are no price hikes. We're all contributing to the cost of the rent the same way. I think Theater Alliance came at this from a place of abundance, where we said, "hey, we're taking on the capital campaign, we're taking on the financial risk, but we want this space to be shared." There's a revenue share model. Rentals are never required for us to meet our bottom line. If there are rentals, it's a bonus for everybody and everybody shares the revenue profit; we consider that a part of the mutual aid principle. It's a collaborative decision-making between the leadership organizations. I do think it's a little bit of a radical model; it's definitely based on some solidarity economics and mutual aid principles.

NL: What would success mean for you a year from now?

SG: 300 nights a year you come in and see a piece of art that you didn't expect to see. That is our dream vision.

This is my first leadership role in a nonprofit organization. I've been an artist, a freelancer, I'm an actor and director, but I think that gives me a perspective that I hope this place is for artists...we built it for artists, to create work in, to collaborate in to cross-pollinate ideas. And that's part of the spillover between the art spaces and the community spaces, it should start to feel interwoven. We believe the arts are a central tenet of a thriving society. Part of the purpose of this building is to be a central tenet in this community--a thriving D.C. arts ecosystem.

NL: I asked her what she was looking forward to most in this grand opening weekend, and she became emotional

SG: The staff is amazing, as well as the donor and patron community that has come out in full force. It is not an easy time in the arts, it's not an easy time in D.C., and we have had such a robust experience with support and advocacy, everything from grass roots donor community to the large philanthropic community, everything from government funding to even working with the developer, there is so much gratitude for all the pro bono help we've gotten. Yes, I'm looking forward to saying thank you to everybody and sharing the space with them.

NL: And we're looking forward to the grand opening festival which kicks off Friday and continues through Tuesday... and most of all, for the opportunity to discover some thought-provoking performances from Theater Alliance, IN Series and 4 Eye Film Center, and just to hang out and absorb the creative vibes with a nice coffee or glass of wine. What a gift to the neighborhood, what a gift to Washington area art lovers.

Revada Arts Center shared by Theater Alliance, INSeries and 4Eye Film Center

Free Opening festival, October 23-27
340 Maple Dr. SW
www.RevadaArtsCenter.org

articles.title: Ariel Quartet Plays Late Beethoven
articles.dek: James Jacobs speaks with Ariel Quartet's violist Jan Grüning about completing their Beethoven cycle with their release of the third and final recording of Beethoven's string quartets.
articles.body:
This month – October 2026 – marks the 200th anniversary of the composition of Beethoven’s final complete work, the String Quartet in F major, Op. 135, and next March is the 200th anniversary of his death. These milestones are part of the reason for the timing of the release of the third and final volume of Beethoven’s quartets by the Ariel Quartet. The cycle has gotten rave reviews in many publications including Gramophone and The New York Times.

The Ariel Quartet was founded in 1998, when its members were teenagers. In 2012 they began their ongoing relationship with the University of Cincinnati College Conservatory of Music, where they serve as faculty quartet-in-residence. That was also the year the quartet had its only personnel change to date when violist Jan Grüning joined the group. He’s definitely committed to it, since he’s married to its cellist Amit Even-Tov and they have three daughters, whom the two violinists, Gershon Gerchikov and Alexandra Kazovsky, know very well. It’s a very tight-knit ensemble – which one has to be to tackle Beethoven’s late quartets.

They are almost frighteningly intimate. It’s telling that after his twin peaks - the Missa Solemnis and the Ninth Symphony - works that required some of the largest musical forces that had ever been assembled up to that time – Beethoven spent the three years remaining to him composing one last cycle of string quartets. It’s a true cycle, with shared themes and references across all five works: the Quartet in E flat, op. 127; the Quartet in a minor, op. 132, which contains the sublime Heiliger Dankgesang (“Holy Song of Thanksgiving”), a musical prayer of gratitude for surviving a severe illness; the Quartet in B flat, op. 130, a massive work in six movements that the Ariel plays with its original finale, the Grosse Fuge, which gave its first listeners a kind of sneak preview of the quartets of Bartok and Shostakovich they would not live long enough to hear; the Quartet in c sharp minor, op, 131 a cyclic work in seven uninterrupted movements that Beethoven declared was his greatest composition; and the Quartet in F major, op. 135, an unexpected return to Haydnesque dimensions, but underneath its classical surface is a work just as deep and mysterious as the others – the finale is based on an inscrutable motif that Beethoven indicates is supposed to evoke the phrase “Muss es sein?” (“Must it be?”), ending his body of work with what is either a profound existential question or a silly joke, or both. (The Ariel decided not to include in this set the alternative finale to op. 130, but they have indicated that it will be included on an upcoming album.)

The Ariel Quartet has been playing the late quartets since the beginning of their career, and one can tell; they fully inhabit this music which they know as well as they know one another.

articles.title: Actor Jamie Wilkes on Playing C.P.E. Bach on STC's The Score
articles.dek: James Jacobs speaks with actor Jamie Wilkes about playing C.P.E. Bach in STC's production of The Score, a play surrounding the musical challenge proposed to J.S. Bach resulting in the Musical Offering.
articles.body:
Jamie Wilkes is currently playing Carl Philip Emanuel Bach in Oliver Cotton’s The Score, currently playing at STC Shakespeare Theatre Company starring Brian Cox as his character’s father Johann Sebastian Bach. He received his professional training at the London Academy of Music and Dramatic Arts – the same school where, half a century earlier, Mr. Cox received his training. This actually helped Wilkes get into character, because he was a long-time admirer of the elder actor’s work and looked up to him as a legend he hoped to emulate, much like CPE Bach’s relationship to JS Bach. That was just one of many fascinating observations he revealed to me in our interview (which you can listen to in the embedded audio). Jamie’s trajectory does in fact bear much resemblance to Brian’s: they have both worked at many of the same theatres and institutions, from the Edinburgh Fringe to the Royal Shakespeare Company, and Jamie has already accrued an impressive body of work in what Americans call “prestige television” and the Brits just call television, including a recurring role on His Dark Materials for HBO/BBC One.

Image Jamie Wilkes as C.P.E. Bach/Photo: Teresa Castracane

In addition to recommending that you listen to the interview, I’m also going to take this opportunity to recommend that you listen to more CPE Bach. He was a major musical figure in his own right who, more than any other single composer, led the transition from the harpsichord to the fortepiano and from the Baroque to the Classical eras. His real-life relationship to his father was, from all documented evidence, a bit frostier than is depicted in the play. JSB made no secret of the fact that he had a favorite son, and that was his eldest, Wilhelm Friedemann Bach. While WF was undeniably brilliant, talented and left behind some impressive works, it’s evident that he crumbled under the weight of his father’s expectations, never found stable employment, succumbed to alcoholism and died in poverty. Whereas CPE toiled away in his nominally prestigious but somewhat thankless position with Frederick the Great, produced what he was asked to without complaint, and organized his father’s papers to the extent that he could, though he noted that thoroughly cataloguing JSB’s compositions would be a full-time job that would leave him no time to compose his own.

A good place to start in exploring CPE’s output is in a trio of works that are in frequent rotation on WETA Classical: the concertos that he wrote in the early 1750s in the wake of his father’s death. Perhaps as a tribute to his father’s penchant for endlessly recycling and re-arranging his own music, CPE provided three different versions of each of these three concertos, so that the solo instrument could be flute, cello or harpsichord while the string accompaniment remains the same. The three concertos form a triptych that uses its temporal vantage point in the mid-18th century to sum up its musical trajectory. The first, in A minor, looks backward to the style of Vivaldi, but with a more spacious sense of development, so that each movement is the length of an entire Vivaldi concerto. The second, in B flat major, seems to be in the here and now of 1751, thoroughly steeped in the galant style favored by his employer the King. The third concerto in A major looks prophetically to the future, anticipating the Classical style of the 1770s and giving CPE an opportunity to shake off his taciturn impulses and produce one of his most freewheeling and deeply felt works.

And, finally, be sure to check out my guided tour of JS Bach’s Musical Offering, only available through the end of October.

articles.title: Pulitzer Prize-Winning Ellen Taaffe Zwilich on Her Music
articles.dek: John Banther speaks with the first woman composer to win the Pulitzer Prize in Music, Ellen Taaffe Zwilich, about her music, including The Peanuts Gallery composed in honor of her feature on the comic strip.
articles.body:
On a recent episode of Classical Breakdown, your guide to classical music, we talked about Peanuts Gallery, a piano concerto by Ellen Taaffe Zwilich, a Pulitzer Prize winning American composer. It brings all the Peanuts characters to life, and in that episode, we learned all about the music and how different art forms come together in culture.

I also recently spoke with this composer, we talked about several of her works, and when you listen to the interview on WETA Virtuoso (see On Air This Week for the schedule), we’ll also hear one of the works afterwards.

articles.title: Damien Geter's Declaration with J'Nai Bridges and Sphinx Virtuosi at Anna H. Wang Concert Series
articles.dek: John Banther speaks with composer Damien Geter about his work Declarations, to be featured on an upcoming program with Anna H Wang Concert Series featuring Sphinx Virtuosi and J'Nai Bridges.
articles.body:
A new work by Damien Geter gets its Washington premiere on October 24 at the Anna H. Wang Concert Series. It’s called Declaration, features J’Nai Bridges with a libretto by Aaron Dworkin, and marks both the 30th anniversary of the Sphynx Organization and the 250th of the United States of America.

Damien and I will give a pre-concert talk this Saturday beforehand to discuss the details, but to get us ready for that and the world premiere, he went ahead and gave us an idea as to what we can expect in this work and each movement.

articles.title: Davóne Tines' Recital No. 1: Mass on Fortas Chamber Music Concerts
articles.dek: Bass-baritone Davóne Tines opens Fortas Chamber Music Concerts with Recital No. 1: MASS, both a recital and theatrical work exploring spirituality, history, identity and renewal.
articles.body:
Bass-baritone Davóne Tines self-describes — quite accurately — as “a singer and creator”, for this artist is more than just an exceptionally gifted vocalist. These qualities will be evident in his performance on Wednesday, October 14 at the Fortas Chamber Music Concerts of his Recital No. 1: MASS. This is a recital, yes, but also a theatrical work, and a personal and communal exploration of spirituality, history, identity and renewal. Tines has performed it at the Ojai Music Festival in 2022. In this Washington performance, he will be joined by pianist John Bitoy III.

Recital No. 1: MASS is not, strictly speaking, a performance of a musical setting of the Roman Catholic Mass Ordinary, though it does contain elements of that tradition — while invoking many other voices, customs, spiritualities and experiences as well. Johann Sebastian Bach makes an appearance, with one of the most beloved arias from the Saint Matthew Passion; Margaret Bonds and Julius Eastman, Black American composers of the 20th century, are represented; compositions by Tyshawn Sorey and Caroline Shaw will be featured.

The concert will be in the Hammer Auditorium, inside the Flagg Building at the Corcoran School of the Arts & Design.
